content: 1. Physical activity (PA) conducted as part of household tasks has been shown to reduce the risk of breast cancer in inactive adults. 2. Total physical activity and leisure-time physical activity have protective effects against osteoporosis in males and females, respectively. 3. To better understand the role of physical activity in preventing chronic diseases in specific regions, future studies should employ longitudinal designs, representative samples, and valid, reliable assessments of various physical activity domains. 4. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) demonstrated that programmed exercise lasting at least six weeks significantly reduces mild to moderate depressive symptoms in women aged 40 and older. 5. The systematic review included searches across multiple databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and SciELO) without language restrictions, focusing on terms such as depression, depressive symptoms, exercise, physical activity, menopause, and randomized controlled trial. 6. Exercise interventions were categorized as mid-term (lasting 12 weeks to 4 months) or long-term (lasting 6–12 months). Changes in depressive symptoms were measured using standardized questionnaires, and effect sizes were calculated using Hedges' g for meta-analysis. 7. The meta-analysis revealed that chronic physical activity significantly improves working memory performance (WMP) in healthy individuals, while acute physical activity does not yield significant effects. 8. The systematic review of RCTs investigating physical activity and WMP included studies published between August 2009 and December 2016, with interventions ranging from cycling to yoga. 9. Chronic physical activity interventions demonstrated a small but significant effect on WMP, while acute interventions showed trivial, non-significant results. Age and intensity were identified as significant moderators of the effects. 10. Workplace health promotion programs targeting sleep duration have shown potential to improve employee sleep and subsequent daytime performance. 11. A systematic review of workplace-based interventions identified 20 studies that measured sleep duration as an outcome, with most interventions utilizing three or fewer behavior change techniques. 12. Physical activity has been shown to protect against the onset of depression, regardless of age or geographical region, as evidenced by a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies. 13. Higher levels of physical activity are associated with reduced risks of anxiety disorders, including agoraphobia and post-traumatic stress disorder, as demonstrated in a meta-analysis of prospective studies. 14. Meeting physical activity guidelines, including aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities, is associated with reduced all-cause, cardiovascular, cancer, and respiratory disease mortality among smokers, based on data from the National Health Interview Surveys linked to the National Death Index. 15. Strength-promoting exercises (SPE), such as gym-based or bodyweight strength activities, are associated with reduced all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality, as shown in pooled analyses of population cohort data from the Health Survey for England and the Scottish Health Survey.
